tools.name: ECC (Everything Claude Code)
tools.whatItDoes: Affaan Mustafa's (affaan-m) harness-native operator system: bundles ~60 specialized agents, ~230 skills, ~75 slash commands, hooks, memory optimization, and a security scanner on top of Claude Code. Cross-harness (also Codex/Cursor/OpenCode/Gemini/Zed/Copilot) via a single AGENTS.md source-of-truth and DRY adapters.
tools.installMethod: Plugin: `/plugin marketplace add https://github.com/affaan-m/ECC` then `/plugin install ecc@ecc`. OR installer with profile: `npx ecc-install --profile minimal --target claude` (also ./install.sh / install.ps1). Rules can be copied project-level into `.claude/rules/ecc/`.
tools.notes: This is the real identity of the user's garbled 'ECC'. NOTE: it is 'embedded' only in the sense of 'embedded across multiple AI harnesses' — NOT embedded/firmware/ESP-IDF. Zero ESP-IDF content. Star counts on the repo (182K+/202K) are internally inconsistent and look inflated — distrust the numbers, not the repo. Plugin install is global to ~/.claude; for strict project-only, prefer copying just the rules into the project's .claude/rules and toggling via enabledPlugins per-project. Heavy/complex; competes for the orchestration role with OMC/Ruflo — pick ONE orchestrator.

tools.name: OMC (oh-my-claudecode)
tools.whatItDoes: Yeachan Heo's 'teams-first' multi-agent orchestration layer for Claude Code ('Don't learn Claude Code. Just use OMC.'). Layers specialized agents + skills via skill injection, smart model routing (Haiku/Sonnet/Opus by task complexity), and a staged Team pipeline (Plan -> PRD -> Exec -> Verify -> Fix). Notably it ships its OWN Ralph mode (`/ralph`) for persistent verify/fix completion loops.
tools.installMethod: Plugin: `/plugin marketplace add https://github.com/Yeachan-Heo/oh-my-claudecode` then `/plugin install oh-my-claudecode`. OR npm: `npm i -g oh-my-claude-sisyphus@latest` (npm name differs from repo). Setup via `/omc-setup`. Skills: project-scope `.omc/skills/` vs user-scope `~/.omc/skills/`.
tools.notes: This is the real identity of the user's garbled 'OMC'. v4.14.4 (May 26 2026), ~35.5k stars, 230 releases — very actively maintained. Of the three big orchestrators (ECC/OMC/Ruflo) this is the lightest-touch and has the cleanest per-project skill scope (.omc/skills/), which fits the user's HARD project-only constraint best. Its built-in Ralph mode means you likely do NOT need the separate Anthropic ralph-wiggum plugin if you adopt OMC. CONFLICTS with ECC and Ruflo: all three want to be 'the orchestrator' and stack hooks/skill-injection — running two simultaneously causes competing delegation/hook behavior. Choose one.

tools.name: Ruflo (formerly claude-flow / 'Ruflo')
tools.whatItDoes: ruvnet's heavyweight swarm orchestration platform (the project formerly called 'claude-flow', now rebranded Ruflo — this is the user's 'Ruflo'). Coordinates large numbers of specialized agents with a queen/topology/consensus swarm model, self-learning memory, 27 hooks, an MCP server with hundreds of tools, and multi-LLM provider support.
tools.installMethod: Plugin (lite, slash-commands only, NO MCP): `/plugin marketplace add ruvnet/ruflo` then `/plugin install ruflo-core@ruflo`. Full CLI: `npx ruflo@latest init wizard` (writes .claude/, .claude-flow/, CLAUDE.md, 27 hooks + daemon into the workspace). MCP: `claude mcp add ruflo -- npx ruflo@latest mcp start`.
tools.notes: Real and very active (v3.10.31, May 31 2026; 6,669 commits). The user's 'Ruflo' = this. BUT it is the heaviest/most invasive option: full CLI install drops a background daemon + 27 hooks that intercept and route tasks, plus a large MCP surface — overkill and risky for a single-dev embedded project, and the daemon/hooks are exactly what can leak into other projects if not carefully scoped. For an ESP-IDF firmware project this is over-engineered. If anything, use only the lite plugin (no MCP/daemon). Recommend AVOID in favor of lighter OMC or plain Superpowers unless the user specifically wants large parallel swarms.

tools.name: ralph-wiggum (Anthropic official plugin)
tools.whatItDoes: Official Anthropic plugin in the anthropics/claude-code repo implementing Geoffrey Huntley's Ralph technique IN-SESSION. Instead of an external `while true` bash loop, it uses a Stop hook to block Claude's exit and re-feed the SAME prompt each iteration until a completion phrase is matched. Commands: `/ralph-loop "<task>" --max-iterations <n> --completion-promise "DONE"` and `/cancel-ralph`.
tools.installMethod: Bundled in anthropics/claude-code plugins dir; install via Claude Code plugin/marketplace mechanism (`/plugin`). Enable per-project via `enabledPlugins` in .claude/settings.json. The raw technique needs no install at all: `while :; do cat PROMPT.md | claude -p; done` in git-bash.
tools.notes: Resolves the user's 'Ralph loop / raphel loop': YES it's real, it IS Geoffrey Huntley's technique (July 2025, ghuntley.com/ralph), and Anthropic shipped an official plugin for it. For embedded/ESP-IDF this is genuinely useful: wrap an iterate-until-`idf.py build` succeeds loop (with --max-iterations as a hard safety net — ALWAYS set it). Caution: an unbounded loop on firmware can burn tokens and make sweeping changes; pair with git checkpoints. If you adopt OMC you already get a Ralph mode and may not need this plugin separately.

tools.name: Superpowers (obra/superpowers)
tools.whatItDoes: Jesse Vincent's (obra) agentic skills framework enforcing brainstorm -> plan -> implement with red/green TDD, subagent-driven development, two-stage self-review, and systematic debugging. Skills auto-trigger by intent. Already installed for this user.
tools.installMethod: `/plugin marketplace add obra/superpowers-marketplace` then `/plugin install superpowers@superpowers-marketplace` (needs Claude Code ~2.0.13+). Restart after install.
tools.notes: Already installed for this user (confirmed in the available skills list: superpowers:brainstorming, executing-plans, TDD, systematic-debugging, etc.). Crossed ~94k stars and was accepted into Anthropic's skills marketplace in 2026 — first-class, lowest-risk choice. Methodology-only (no swarm/daemon), so it does NOT conflict with a single chosen orchestrator and actually composes well. For a competition embedded project, the brainstorming + writing-plans + TDD + verification-before-completion skills are the highest-leverage, lowest-footprint pieces. KEEP this as the spine; add at most ONE orchestrator on top.

tools.name: SuperClaude (SuperClaude-Org/SuperClaude_Framework)
tools.whatItDoes: A configuration framework that injects behavioral instructions (.md) to add /sc: commands, cognitive personas, and a brainstorm->design->workflow->implement->test methodology. v4.1.x/4.2.0; TS plugin system planned for v5.
tools.installMethod: `pipx install SuperClaude && SuperClaude install` (or pip, or `npm install -g @bifrost_inc/superclaude && superclaude install`, or clone + ./install.sh).
tools.notes: Real and popular, but overlaps heavily with Superpowers (both are brainstorm/plan/implement/test methodology layers). Running both = duplicated/competing /sc: vs superpowers: command surfaces and conflicting workflow injection. Since the user ALREADY has Superpowers, adding SuperClaude is redundant. Its installer is more global-oriented (pipx/pip/npm -g + SuperClaude install) which fits the project-only constraint poorly. Skip unless replacing Superpowers.

tools.notes: A pick-and-choose agent library rather than an orchestrator, so it composes without the 'two orchestrators fight' problem. Useful if the user wants a specific specialist (e.g., code-reviewer, security) without adopting a whole harness. No verified embedded/ESP-IDF specialist found.

tools.notes: Real but built for massive parallel sweeps on large codebases — wrong shape for a single-dev embedded firmware project. tmux-based external orchestration also fits poorly on Windows+git-bash. Avoid for this use case.

keyAnswers.question: What is ECC and is it a real installable Claude Code framework?
keyAnswers.answer: ECC = 'Everything Claude Code' by Affaan Mustafa (github.com/affaan-m/ECC). YES, it is real and installable: `/plugin marketplace add https://github.com/affaan-m/ECC` then `/plugin install ecc@ecc`, or `npx ecc-install --profile minimal --target claude`. It is a harness-native operator system bundling ~60 agents, ~230 skills, ~75 commands, hooks, memory optimization, and a security scanner. CRITICAL CLARIFICATION: it is 'embedded' only in the sense of being embedded ACROSS multiple AI harnesses (Codex/Cursor/etc.) — it has ZERO embedded/firmware/ESP-IDF content, so it does not directly help an ESP32-S3 workflow. It can be scoped per-project (copy rules into .claude/rules/ecc + toggle via enabledPlugins), but the default plugin install is global to ~/.claude. Its advertised star counts (182K/202K) are internally inconsistent and look inflated — trust the repo, distrust the metrics.

keyAnswers.question: What is OMC and what does it conflict with?
keyAnswers.answer: OMC = 'oh-my-claudecode' by Yeachan Heo (github.com/yeachan-heo/oh-my-claudecode), a real, very actively maintained (v4.14.4, May 2026, ~35.5k stars) teams-first multi-agent orchestration layer with smart model routing (Haiku/Sonnet/Opus) and a staged Team pipeline. Install: `/plugin marketplace add https://github.com/Yeachan-Heo/oh-my-claudecode` then `/plugin install oh-my-claudecode`. It CONFLICTS with the other 'whole-harness orchestrators' — ECC, Ruflo, and SuperClaude — because all of them try to be THE orchestrator and stack their own hooks/skill-injection/delegation; running two at once causes competing behavior. It does NOT meaningfully conflict with Superpowers (methodology-only) and in fact OMC bundles its own Ralph mode, so it overlaps with the standalone ralph-wiggum plugin. Of the three big orchestrators, OMC has the cleanest per-project scope (.omc/skills/), best fitting the user's project-only constraint.

keyAnswers.question: Is the 'Ralph/ralph loop' a real technique and what is it?
keyAnswers.answer: YES, real and well-documented. The Ralph loop is Geoffrey Huntley's agentic technique (canonical post: ghuntley.com/ralph, July 2025), named after Simpsons' Ralph Wiggum for its 'dumb but persistent' quality. In its purest form it is a bash loop — `while :; do cat PROMPT.md | claude -p; done` — that re-feeds the SAME prompt each iteration; state survives via the codebase/TODO file/git, and each fresh-context pass self-reviews and refines. Anthropic shipped an OFFICIAL plugin implementing it in-session (anthropics/claude-code plugins/ralph-wiggum), using a Stop hook to block exit and re-feed the prompt: `/ralph-loop "<task>" --max-iterations <n> --completion-promise "DONE"`. ALWAYS set --max-iterations as a safety net. For ESP-IDF it's useful as an 'iterate until idf.py build/flash succeeds' loop — pair with git checkpoints to bound blast radius. Note: OMC already bundles a /ralph mode, so adopting OMC may make the standalone plugin redundant.

keyAnswers.question: Given the project-only HARD constraint, which orchestrator should be chosen and how is per-project scoping actually enforced?
keyAnswers.answer: Pick ONE orchestrator, not several — ECC, OMC, and Ruflo are mutually conflicting. Best fit for a single-dev ESP-IDF project under a strict project-only constraint: keep Superpowers (already installed, methodology spine, lowest footprint) + optionally add OMC (lightest orchestrator, native .omc/skills/ project scope) + optionally the ralph-wiggum loop for build-fix iteration. AVOID Ruflo (heavy daemon + 27 hooks that are hardest to keep from leaking into other projects). Per-project enforcement in Claude Code: (a) project MCP servers in .mcp.json gated by enabledMcpjsonServers/disabledMcpjsonServers in .claude/settings.json; (b) plugins toggled per-project via `enabledPlugins`: {"plugin@marketplace": true} in .claude/settings.json. IMPORTANT LIMITATION (anthropics/claude-code issue #11461): plugin enablement does NOT auto-switch by directory — you may still need `/plugin enable|disable` when entering the project. So for true isolation, prefer tools whose payload lives in the repo (.omc/skills/, .claude/rules/, .mcp.json) and avoid global daemons.

keyAnswers.question: Did the prior AI plan likely contain hallucinations, and what is the recommended truth-filter going forward?
keyAnswers.answer: The four named items all resolved to REAL tools once de-garbled (ECC=Everything Claude Code, OMC=oh-my-claudecode, Ruflo=former claude-flow, Ralph loop=Huntley's technique + official ralph-wiggum plugin), so the prior plan's NAMES were real — but its likely fabrications are in the DETAILS: invented sub-repos, wrong/inflated version and star claims (ECC's own page shows inconsistent 182K vs 202K stars), and 'embedded' being misread as firmware/ESP-IDF when ECC's 'embedded' means cross-harness. Going forward, vet every tool against hesreallyhim/awesome-claude-code (canonical curated list, non-working tools get cut) and confirm install commands + last-release date on the actual GitHub repo before trusting any AI-supplied plan.

dimension: General-purpose MCP servers for a strong project-level Claude Code coding harness (embedded ESP-IDF / ESP32-S3 focus)

tools.name: Serena (oraios/serena)
tools.whatItDoes: Language-server-protocol-backed MCP that gives the agent IDE-grade semantic tools (find_symbol, find_referencing_symbols, insert_after_symbol, replace_symbol_body) so it edits at the symbol level instead of grepping whole files. Free, no API key, runs LSP locally. For C/C++ it uses clangd. Per-project: it reads a compile_commands.json from the project root and indexes only that repo.
tools.installMethod: uvx from GitHub (recommended by maintainers). .mcp.json stdio entry: command "uvx", args ["--from","git+https://github.com/oraios/serena","serena","start-mcp-server","--context","ide-assistant","--project","${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.}"]. Maintainers explicitly warn NOT to install via MCP marketplaces (stale commands).
tools.notes: Latest release ~v1.5.3 (late May, MIT, VS Code/MS/GitHub OSPO sponsored). The ONE genuinely additive tool here: codegraphcontext + context7 do NOT do LSP-backed semantic EDITING. For a C/ESP-IDF codebase, clangd (with compile_commands.json that ESP-IDF/CMake already emits in build/) gives real cross-reference + rename across the firmware. Caveat: clangd needs the compile DB; point CLANGD at the IDF toolchain. Project-scope it via --project flag so it never indexes the user's other repos. Worth adding.

tools.name: GitHub MCP server (github/github-mcp-server)
tools.whatItDoes: GitHub's official MCP server (Go, rewritten from Anthropic's original reference). Reads repos, manages issues/PRs, monitors Actions CI runs, analyzes build failures, code scanning + Dependabot alerts. Two modes: remote hosted (https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/, OAuth/PAT) or local Docker (ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server).
tools.installMethod: EASIEST for Claude Code is the remote HTTP server, NOT stdio: claude mcp add --transport http github https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/ --header "Authorization: Bearer <PAT>". For pure project-scope + stdio, use local Docker. Note: a remote HTTP server cannot be cleanly pinned to one project via .mcp.json the way a stdio server can, but you can still put the http entry in the project .mcp.json so it only loads for this repo.
tools.notes: Useful only if the competition project lives on GitHub and the user wants CI/PR/issue automation. For a solo embedded comp repo this is mostly overkill vs. just using the gh CLI / git. Recommend 'optional'. Requires a GitHub PAT (fine-grained, scoped to the one repo) which keeps it project-bounded. Do NOT confuse with the user's existing 'gitnexus' (different tool).

tools.name: Filesystem MCP (@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem)
tools.whatItDoes: Anthropic-maintained reference server: read/write/edit files, list dirs, move/rename, metadata, all gated to a configurable allow-list of directories (or MCP Roots). Node.js.
tools.installMethod: npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem <allowed-dir>. .mcp.json: command "npx", args ["-y","@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem","${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.}"]. Passing only the project dir naturally scopes file access to this project.
tools.notes: REDUNDANT for Claude Code: the CLI already has native Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep with full filesystem access. An MCP filesystem server adds nothing and burns context with duplicate tools. The directory allow-list is its only marginal value (sandboxing), but Claude Code's permission system covers that. Recommend AVOID unless you specifically want hard directory sandboxing.

tools.name: Desktop Commander (wonderwhy-er/DesktopCommanderMCP)
tools.whatItDoes: MCP server giving the agent terminal control: execute shell commands, manage long-running processes/REPLs, paginated process output, diff-based file edits, search. Configurable shell (bash/zsh/powershell), blockedCommands list, allowedDirectories.
tools.installMethod: npx @wonderwhy-er/desktop-commander@latest setup, or .mcp.json stdio: command "npx", args ["-y","@wonderwhy-er/desktop-commander"]. ~5.3k stars, MIT, updated Jan 2026 (active).
tools.notes: REDUNDANT and arguably risky for Claude Code: the CLI already has a first-class Bash tool plus background processes and the Monitor tool. Desktop Commander was built primarily for Claude DESKTOP (which has no terminal). Its allowedDirectories does NOT constrain terminal commands (per its own docs terminal can reach outside), so it is poorly project-scopable. For an ESP-IDF flow (idf.py build/flash/monitor) the native Bash tool is better integrated. Recommend AVOID on Claude Code.

tools.name: Git MCP (modelcontextprotocol/git, pkg mcp-server-git)
tools.category: Git repository operations MCP (official reference server)
tools.whatItDoes: Python reference server: git status, diff, log (with flexible date filters), add/commit/reset, branch create/checkout, init. Scoped to a single --repository path.
tools.installMethod: uvx mcp-server-git --repository <path>. .mcp.json stdio: command "uvx", args ["mcp-server-git","--repository","${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.}"]. The --repository flag pins it to one repo = naturally project-scoped. Also pip-installable (mcp-server-git on PyPI) or Docker (mcp/git).
tools.notes: REDUNDANT: Claude Code drives git perfectly via the Bash tool, and the user ALREADY has 'gitnexus' globally. The official mcp-server-git is explicitly 'early development, tools subject to change' and lacks push/pull/merge. No reason to add over native git + existing gitnexus. Recommend AVOID. (Third-party cyanheads/git-mcp-server is more complete with push/pull/merge/rebase/worktree if a git MCP were truly wanted, but it still duplicates native capability.)

keyAnswers.question: Exact .mcp.json schema/example to add a stdio MCP server scoped to one project in Claude Code
Is Serena worth adding given the user already has codegraphcontext + context7?
keyAnswers.answer: Yes — it is the single most additive server in this set, because it does something the existing two do NOT: LSP-backed semantic EDITING and precise cross-reference navigation at the symbol level. context7 = external library DOCS lookup (no view of the user's own code). codegraphcontext = a code-graph/relationship index for retrieval/understanding, but not a clangd-driven find_referencing_symbols + replace_symbol_body editing toolset. Serena runs clangd against the project's compile_commands.json (ESP-IDF/CMake already emits this under build/), giving accurate 'who calls this function', rename, and symbol-scoped edits across the firmware — valuable in a multi-file C codebase with HAL/driver layers. Net recommendation: SHOULD add, project-scoped with --project ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.} and --context ide-assistant. Two caveats: (a) C/C++ semantic accuracy depends on a valid compile_commands.json + clangd seeing the Xtensa toolchain includes, so it needs a little setup; (b) there is mild functional overlap with codegraphcontext for pure 'understand the code' queries, so the justification for Serena is editing/refactoring, not read-only search.

keyAnswers.question: Which of the user's 8 existing global MCPs are most useful vs redundant for embedded C/ESP-IDF work?
keyAnswers.answer: MOST USEFUL for embedded ESP32-S3/ESP-IDF: (1) embedded-debugger — the standout: probe-rs-based flash/RTT/breakpoints/memory ops on real hardware; directly supports the flash+debug loop. NOTE one mismatch to flag: its description lists ARM Cortex-M and RISC-V, while the target here is ESP32-S3 = Xtensa LX7, which probe-rs does NOT support — so for the S3 this MCP is likely NOT usable over JTAG; it would only apply to a RISC-V ESP (C3/C6/P4) or an ARM probe. Verify before relying on it. (2) context7 — high value for pulling current ESP-IDF v5.5 / component API docs instead of stale training data. (3) sequential-thinking — useful for planning the architecture refactor. (4) memory — useful for persisting the project context across sessions (already in use per MEMORY.md). MODERATE: codegraphcontext (code understanding of the firmware tree). LOWER PRIORITY / borderline-redundant for embedded C: (5) playwright — browser automation, irrelevant to firmware unless testing a web dashboard; (6) taskmaster-ai — project/task planning, overlaps with Claude Code's own TaskCreate/TaskList and the user's MEMORY workflow; (7) gitnexus — git ops that native Bash+git already cover, and it makes the proposed git MCP fully redundant. Bottom line: keep embedded-debugger (if target is RISC-V/ARM), context7, sequential-thinking, memory as the core; treat playwright/taskmaster-ai/gitnexus as redundant-for-embedded. And do NOT add the filesystem, shell (desktop-commander), or git MCPs proposed in the prior plan — all three duplicate native Claude Code tools and/or gitnexus.

tools.name: Espressif Documentation MCP Server
tools.whatItDoes: Official Espressif-hosted remote MCP server. Exposes a single tool search_espressif_sources(query, language) that does semantic retrieval over the live Espressif docs corpus (datasheets, API refs, migration/HW-design guides) and returns text fragments with source URLs. Reduces hallucination by grounding answers in current official docs.
tools.installMethod: claude mcp add --transport http "espressif-documentation" "https://mcp.espressif.com/docs"  (project-scope it with: claude mcp add -s project ... which writes to .mcp.json)
tools.notes: REAL and official. Prior plan's claims hold up: GitHub/WeChat OAuth on first connect, designed for interactive use not CI/batch (a per-hr/per-day rate-limit posture is stated as 'not for bulk automation' — exact 40/hr 200/day numbers I did NOT see verbatim on the dev-portal page, treat those specific figures as unverified). Endpoint https://mcp.espressif.com/docs returns 405 to plain GET (it speaks MCP HTTP transport, not browser GET) — that 405 is EXPECTED, not a sign it's broken. For your hard project-level constraint, add with -s project so it lands in ./.mcp.json and never touches other projects. This is the single highest-value, lowest-risk addition for your harness.

tools.name: ESP-IDF Tools local MCP server (idf.py mcp-server)
tools.whatItDoes: stdio MCP server built into idf.py that exposes set_target / build / flash / device-list / status as MCP tools+resources, letting Claude Code drive the set_target -> build -> flash loop in natural language.
tools.installMethod: Requires ESP-IDF v6.0+. Start via: idf.py mcp-server (from an activated IDF env in a project dir), or eim run "idf.py mcp-server" (EIM >= 0.8.1, no shell activation needed). Then register the stdio command in .mcp.json.
tools.notes: CRITICAL VERSION FINDING — the prior plan was CORRECT here: this feature was introduced in ESP-IDF v6.0 and is ABSENT in your installed v5.5.4. Confirmed against the dev-portal article and the v6.0 Programming Guide (idf.py page). So on your current 5.5.4 toolchain you CANNOT run idf.py mcp-server. Two paths: (1) build a small local stdio MCP 'idf.py bridge' yourself (wrap idf.py build/flash + a non-blocking monitor — note idf.py monitor is a long-running blocking stream, so a bridge must run it as a background subprocess and buffer lines for polling); or (2) upgrade to ESP-IDF v6.0+ (separate side-by-side install via EIM, won't disturb 5.5.4) and enable the 'mcp' feature at install time. Given your project-isolation constraint, a self-contained local bridge script checked into the repo is the cleanest 5.5.4 answer. Also: you already have an embedded-debugger MCP (probe-rs based) in this environment which covers flash/RTT/breakpoints for SWD/JTAG — but probe-rs targets ARM/RISC-V and your ESP32-S3 is Xtensa LX7, so that MCP likely will NOT connect to your S3; rely on idf.py-based flashing instead.

tools.name: espressif/esp-claw
tools.whatItDoes: Espressif's 'Chat-Coding' on-device AI agent runtime for IoT. Runs the sense->reason->decide->act loop locally on ESP32-S3; acts as both MCP server and MCP client; on-chip long-term memory; saves confirmed behaviors as deterministic local Lua scripts; Telegram/QQ/Feishu/WeChat integrations; LLM-backed (OpenAI/Qwen/etc).
tools.installMethod: git clone https://github.com/espressif/esp-claw && idf.py build && idf.py flash (or Web Flasher). Needs >=8MB flash + 8MB PSRAM.
tools.notes: REAL and official (corroborated by CNX-Software 2026-04-23, Elektor, esp-claw.com, M5Stack fork, ~1.3k stars). Currently ESP32-S3 only (P4 'coming soon') — matches your target chip. This is a FIRMWARE/product framework (puts an agent ON the device), NOT a dev-assist harness tool for Claude Code. Relevant only if your competition entry itself wants on-device agentic behavior; not part of the build/flash/doc tooling you're assembling. Don't confuse it with your harness.

tools.name: memovai/mimiclaw
tools.category: Community on-device AI agent (OpenClaw on ESP32)
tools.whatItDoes: Runs an OpenClaw-style pocket AI agent in pure C on an ESP32-S3 (16MB flash/8MB PSRAM, ~0.5W). Telegram UX, ReAct tool loop (web search, cron), plain-text on-chip memory files (SOUL.md/USER.md/MEMORY.md), Anthropic+OpenAI providers, OTA, dual-core. MIT.
tools.installMethod: git clone https://github.com/memovai/mimiclaw (firmware build)
tools.notes: REAL: 5.5k stars, v0.1.1 (Mar 2026). Like esp-claw, this is on-device agent FIRMWARE, not a Claude Code harness component. Interesting prior art if your project wants an on-device agent angle; irrelevant to build/flash/doc dev tooling. Note the MEMORY.md/USER.md naming coincidence with your own Claude memory files is just convention.

tools.name: espressif/esp-dl
tools.whatItDoes: Lightweight neural-network inference framework for ESP-series chips. Quantized CNN/Transformer ops with Xtensa/RISC-V assembly kernels; per-channel quant for Conv/Gemm; dual-core scheduling on S3.
tools.installMethod: Add as an ESP-IDF component (idf component / git submodule) in your project — project-local by nature.
tools.notes: REAL: ~1k stars, Release v3.2.0 (Oct 2025), explicitly supports ESP32-S3 and P4. This is a runtime DL library, NOT AI tooling for the dev harness. Directly relevant to your competition project though: your battery-recognition vision currently runs on OpenMV — if you ever want to move inference onto the S3 itself, ESP-DL is the official path. You are on a native ESP-IDF v5.5.4 installer build (idf.py), NOT PlatformIO — so this is OFF-PATH for your toolchain and would add a parallel build system. Skip unless you migrate to PlatformIO. tools.name: espressif/esp-rainmaker-mcp

keyAnswers.question: Is the official Espressif Docs MCP real and what is its exact Claude Code add command?
keyAnswers.answer: YES, real and official. Remote HTTP MCP at https://mcp.espressif.com/docs exposing one tool, search_espressif_sources(query, language), for semantic search over live Espressif docs. Exact command: `claude mcp add --transport http "espressif-documentation" "https://mcp.espressif.com/docs"`. For your project-only constraint, add with project scope so it writes to ./.mcp.json instead of global config: `claude mcp add -s project --transport http espressif-documentation https://mcp.espressif.com/docs`. First call triggers GitHub/WeChat OAuth and a Claude Code allow-tool prompt (or pre-allow with --allowedTools mcp__espressif-documentation__search_espressif_sources). It is for interactive use, not CI/bulk. (A plain browser GET returns HTTP 405 — that is expected MCP-transport behavior, not an outage.)

keyAnswers.question: Does ESP-IDF 5.5.4 ship any official MCP server, or must we build a local idf.py bridge?
keyAnswers.answer: NO — v5.5.4 ships NO official MCP server. The official ESP-IDF Tools local MCP server (idf.py mcp-server, also startable via `eim run "idf.py mcp-server"`) was introduced in ESP-IDF v6.0 and is ABSENT in 5.5.4 (the prior plan was correct on this point). On 5.5.4 you must either (a) build/adopt a local stdio idf.py bridge — write a small wrapper, or vet+pin the community horw/esp-mcp which already does this — making sure to run the blocking `idf.py monitor` as a buffered background subprocess; or (b) install ESP-IDF v6.0+ side-by-side via EIM (won't disturb your 5.5.4) and enable the 'mcp' feature. For strict project isolation, a self-contained bridge script committed to the repo + registered in ./.mcp.json is the cleanest path on 5.5.4.

dimension: Best AI-drivable closed-loop debugging path for ESP32-S3 (Xtensa) under ESP-IDF 5.5.4 on Windows

tools.name: probe-rs (Xtensa/ESP32-S3 support)
tools.whatItDoes: Rust-native debug+flash host. As of 2024+ it DOES support ESP32-S3 Xtensa: connect, halt/resume, flash (incl. octal flash), hardware breakpoints, GDB stub, and RTT — over the S3 built-in USB-JTAG, no external probe. Refutes the 'suspected NO for Xtensa' assumption.
tools.installMethod: cargo install probe-rs-tools, or bundled inside the embedded-debugger MCP
tools.notes: VERIFIED it works for S3 — but recommend AVOID for THIS project. Reason: probe-rs RTT only reads an RTT control block emitted by Rust crates (defmt-rtt / rtt-target). Standard ESP-IDF C logging (ESP_LOGx / printf / ESP_EARLY_LOGx) goes over UART/USB-serial and emits NO RTT block, so probe-rs shows nothing ('No RTT header info present in the ELF file'). For a C/ESP-IDF project the OpenOCD+idf.py path is strictly better and is the Espressif-supported one. Also: known S3 flash-verify failures (#2338, #3637) sometimes require erasing with espflash first. Keep probe-rs only if you later write Rust firmware.

tools.name: embedded-debugger MCP (existing, probe-rs-backed)
tools.whatItDoes: The user's already-installed MCP. Its own server instructions advertise 'ARM Cortex-M, RISC-V, and other architectures via probe-rs' — Xtensa is NOT named. Exposes connect/halt/run/reset/read_memory/breakpoints/rtt_*/flash_* tools.
tools.installMethod: already installed (global MCP)
tools.notes: Two concrete doubts for S3: (1) its description omits Xtensa, and whether the bundled probe-rs binary is new enough to carry the S3 Xtensa flash algorithms is unverified — `probe-rs --version` is not even on PATH in this shell, so I could not confirm the bundled version supports S3. (2) Even if connect/halt/read_memory work, its rtt_read tools will NOT capture ESP-IDF C logs (same RTT-block limitation as raw probe-rs). KEY ANSWER: do not rely on this MCP as the S3 debug path. Its read_memory/halt could in principle peek at S3 RAM if it connects, but that is a fragile bonus, not the loop. Treat as RISC-V-oriented; for S3 use OpenOCD.

tools.name: OpenOCD — Espressif fork (openocd-esp32, bundled with ESP-IDF)
tools.category: JTAG debug host (the correct S3 path)
tools.whatItDoes: Espressif's OpenOCD fork with Xtensa support. Ships INSIDE ESP-IDF 5.5 (already installed at D:\WJ\Espressif). Debugs S3 over the chip's built-in USB-Serial-JTAG with zero external hardware using board/esp32s3-builtin.cfg. Backs GDB (xtensa-esp32s3-elf-gdb), apptrace, SystemView, and gcov-over-JTAG.
tools.installMethod: already present — verify with `openocd --version`; launch via `idf.py openocd` / `idf.py openocd gdb`
tools.notes: This is THE probe-based path for S3, and it is already installed (no new install, satisfies project-scope constraint trivially). Upstream stock OpenOCD has no Xtensa — only this fork does. Built-in USB-JTAG of S3 is sufficient (board/esp32s3-builtin.cfg); no ESP-Prog needed (though an ESP-Prog adds an isolated JTAG if the native USB is flaky). idf.py exposes `idf.py openocd`, `idf.py gdb`, `idf.py gdbtui`, `idf.py gdbgui`. AI-automation: OpenOCD speaks GDB/MI and a Tcl command port (telnet 4444) — both are scriptable and parseable. For an MCP, wrapping `idf.py openocd` + a GDB/MI batch script is more reliable for S3 than probe-rs.

tools.name: idf.py monitor (auto addr2line backtrace decoding)
tools.category: Serial console + automatic crash decode (no probe)
tools.whatItDoes: Reads UART/USB-serial console. On a panic it auto-runs addr2line against build/<proj>.elf and annotates the backtrace with function names + file:line. No JTAG, no extra tools. This is the single most AI-parseable signal in the whole loop.
tools.installMethod: ships with ESP-IDF; run `idf.py -p <PORT> monitor`
tools.notes: AI-automation tip: monitor is interactive (Ctrl-]) and can hang an agent. For a closed loop, prefer capturing with a timeout to a file the agent Reads: e.g. `idf.py flash` then a bounded serial capture (python esp-idf-monitor with --timeout, or `idf.py monitor` killed after N seconds, or pyserial). Decoding requires the flashed ELF to match build/ — always flash+capture from the same build. ESP_MONITOR_DECODE=0 turns decoding off (keep it ON).

tools.name: ESP-IDF Core Dump (flash partition) + idf.py coredump-debug / coredump-info
tools.whatItDoes: On panic, writes a full snapshot (all FreeRTOS task stacks, registers, panic reason) to a coredump flash partition. `idf.py coredump-info` prints a text summary; `idf.py coredump-debug` opens a full GDB session on the frozen state (bt, frame, info locals).
tools.installMethod: enable once in menuconfig (Core Dump -> Flash, ELF format); then automatic
tools.notes: Richer than the live backtrace — every task, not just the faulting one. coredump-info/-debug output is clean text an agent can parse. Requires a coredump partition in partitions.csv (default tables usually include one). This is the best 'why did it crash' signal WITHOUT a probe and pairs perfectly with monitor's live decode.

tools.name: GDBStub on panic / runtime (CONFIG_ESP_SYSTEM_GDBSTUB_RUNTIME)
tools.whatItDoes: A target-side GDB server over the serial line. Panic mode: on crash the stub emits a marker and idf.py monitor auto-launches GDB. Runtime mode: Ctrl-C over serial breaks into a live GDB session. Read memory/vars, examine call stack — without any JTAG hardware.
tools.installMethod: menuconfig: CONFIG_ESP_SYSTEM_PANIC=GDBStub-on-panic and/or CONFIG_ESP_SYSTEM_GDBSTUB_RUNTIME=y
tools.notes: Bridges the gap when you want live single-step/inspection but have no probe. Limited vs full OpenOCD JTAG (no hardware watchpoints, stub runs on the crashed core). Good 'middle tier'. Drive it with GDB batch scripts (-x file -batch) so an agent gets deterministic text output instead of an interactive prompt.

tools.name: ESP-IDF App Trace (apptrace) + SystemView + gcov-over-JTAG
tools.whatItDoes: Streams logs/events/coverage host<->target over JTAG via OpenOCD. esp_apptrace_vprintf redirects ESP_LOGx to host (logtrace_proc.py); CONFIG_APPTRACE_SV_ENABLE produces SystemView traces; gcov dumps .gcda coverage over JTAG at runtime.
tools.installMethod: menuconfig App Trace -> Trace destination JTAG; needs OpenOCD running
tools.notes: This is the 'RTT equivalent that actually works for ESP-IDF C' — non-blocking host logging over JTAG, the proper answer to 'can I get RTT-style logging on S3 in C?'. Requires OpenOCD (and thus a working JTAG, built-in USB-JTAG is fine). Limitation: no tracing from ESP_EARLY_LOGx, and printf args >4 bytes unsupported. Heavier to set up than monitor/coredump; reserve for timing-sensitive or coverage work, not the default loop.

tools.name: videocapture-mcp (13rac1) — webcam still-capture MCP
tools.whatItDoes: FastMCP/OpenCV server exposing quick_capture and connection tools; returns a frame the model can see. Lets the agent 'look' at LEDs / servo position / cut result on the board.
tools.installMethod: git clone https://github.com/13rac1/videocapture-mcp + uv/pip; register via `claude mcp add`
tools.notes: Real MIT-licensed repo, but small/low-maintenance (a third-party review rated it 4/10, limited scope). For project-scope + control I recommend NOT depending on it and instead writing a ~15-line FastMCP cv2 server (returns mcp Image) committed into the project's .claude/, OR — simplest of all — skip MCP entirely: a one-shot capture to a JPG file (e.g. ffmpeg/opencv writing capture.jpg) that Claude Code Reads natively. Claude Code already renders image files via Read, so the MCP only buys 'capture on demand without a shell step'. On Windows, cv2.VideoCapture(0) with the DSHOW/MSMF backend; ensure no other app holds the camera.

tools.name: Custom minimal FastMCP cv2 capture server (DIY)
tools.whatItDoes: ~15 lines: @mcp.tool() capture() -> Image that grabs one webcam frame with cv2 and returns it as an MCP image content type so the model sees it directly. Self-contained, lives in the project's .claude/.
tools.installMethod: pip install 'mcp[cli]' opencv-python numpy; add to project .mcp.json
tools.notes: Recommended over the third-party MCP because it is auditable, project-scoped via .mcp.json, and trivially adaptable (crop ROI to the servo/LED, force a backend, set exposure). The FastMCP Image return type is the load-bearing detail — without returning Image content the model cannot see the frame. If you want zero MCP surface, the file-on-disk + Read approach is the most robust of all (no MCP process to crash) and is what I'd default to.

keyAnswers.question: Can probe-rs / the existing embedded-debugger MCP debug ESP32-S3? yes/no + why
keyAnswers.answer: probe-rs: YES, technically — contrary to the 'suspected NO' assumption. Since ~2024 probe-rs has real Xtensa support (issue #2001): it can connect, halt/resume, flash (incl. octal), set hardware breakpoints, and run GDB on the S3 over its built-in USB-JTAG. HOWEVER for THIS project it is the wrong tool: probe-rs RTT only reads an RTT control block emitted by Rust crates (defmt-rtt/rtt-target); standard ESP-IDF C logging (ESP_LOGx/printf) goes over serial and is INVISIBLE to probe-rs ('No RTT header info present'). The existing embedded-debugger MCP: treat as effectively NO for the S3 loop — its own instructions advertise only 'ARM Cortex-M, RISC-V, and other architectures' (Xtensa not named), the bundled probe-rs version/flash-algo support for S3 is unverified (probe-rs isn't even on PATH in this environment), and even on a successful connect it cannot read C-firmware logs. Net: don't build the S3 debug loop on probe-rs/that MCP; use Espressif's OpenOCD + idf.py instead.

keyAnswers.question: Recommended hardware-in-loop debug path for S3 WITH a JTAG probe?
keyAnswers.answer: Use the Espressif OpenOCD fork (openocd-esp32) that is ALREADY bundled in ESP-IDF 5.5 — no new install. The S3's built-in USB-Serial-JTAG is sufficient (board/esp32s3-builtin.cfg), so 'with a probe' usually means just the existing USB cable; an external ESP-Prog is optional for isolation/reliability. Launch via `idf.py openocd` and `idf.py gdb` (xtensa-esp32s3-elf-gdb). For AI automation, drive GDB in batch/MI mode (gdb -x script.gdb -batch) or OpenOCD's Tcl/telnet 4444 port — both produce deterministic, parseable text. This unlocks hardware breakpoints/watchpoints, memory inspection, plus apptrace/SystemView/gcov-over-JTAG and the proper 'RTT-style' non-blocking host logging for C (esp_apptrace_vprintf), which probe-rs cannot give a C project.

keyAnswers.question: Recommended hardware-in-loop debug path for S3 WITHOUT a JTAG probe?
keyAnswers.answer: The fully serial, no-probe loop — and this should be the AI's DEFAULT because it is the most automatable and needs zero extra hardware: (1) `idf.py build flash`; (2) capture the serial console with a bounded timeout to a file (idf.py monitor auto-decodes panic backtraces via addr2line into function+file:line — keep ESP_MONITOR_DECODE on); (3) enable Core Dump -> Flash (ELF) once, then on any crash run `idf.py coredump-info` (text summary of every task) or `idf.py coredump-debug` (full GDB on the frozen snapshot); (4) optionally enable GDBStub-on-panic so monitor auto-drops into a GDB session over serial for live inspection. All four emit clean text an agent can parse; the addr2line-decoded backtrace + coredump pair is the highest-signal, lowest-setup crash diagnosis available. Automation caveat: idf.py monitor is interactive — run it with a timeout / kill after N seconds (or use pyserial) so the agent doesn't hang waiting on Ctrl-].

keyAnswers.question: Simplest reliable way to give the agent 'eyes' on the board
keyAnswers.answer: Two real options, both verified. SIMPLEST/MOST ROBUST: skip MCP — capture one webcam frame to a JPG on disk (opencv/ffmpeg one-liner) and let Claude Code Read it; Claude Code already renders image files natively, so there's no MCP process to crash and it's trivially project-scoped. SLIGHTLY RICHER: a tiny self-written FastMCP + cv2 server (~15 lines) with an @mcp.tool() capture() -> Image that returns the frame as an MCP image content type, registered in the project's .mcp.json. The load-bearing detail is returning the FastMCP `Image` type so the model actually sees the frame. There IS a real third-party server (13rac1/videocapture-mcp, MIT) but it's small/low-maintenance (a review rated it 4/10), so prefer the DIY version or the file+Read approach for project-scope and control. On Windows use cv2.VideoCapture(0, cv2.CAP_DSHOW) and make sure no other app holds the camera. Tip: crop to the LED/servo ROI before returning to make the visual judgment more reliable.

keyAnswers.question: Does OpenOCD support S3 JTAG, built-in USB-Serial-JTAG, RTT, and apptrace?
keyAnswers.answer: Yes to all except stock RTT. The Espressif OpenOCD fork (bundled with IDF) supports S3 JTAG via the built-in USB-Serial-JTAG (board/esp32s3-builtin.cfg, no external adapter). It supports apptrace over JTAG, SystemView traces (CONFIG_APPTRACE_SV_ENABLE), host log redirection (esp_apptrace_vprintf), and gcov-over-JTAG runtime coverage dumps. 'RTT' in the SEGGER sense isn't the ESP-IDF idiom — the equivalent non-blocking host logging for C is apptrace, not RTT. So for a C/ESP-IDF S3 project, apptrace (OpenOCD) is the correct answer to 'I want RTT-like logging', NOT probe-rs RTT.

dimension: Claude Code harness mechanics for strict project-level isolation and safety

tools.name: .mcp.json (project-scoped MCP config)
tools.whatItDoes: A JSON file at the project root that registers MCP servers under a top-level "mcpServers" key. Committed to git, it gives every clone the same servers WITHOUT touching the user's global config. This is THE mechanism for project-scoped MCP.
tools.installMethod: Create .mcp.json at repo root by hand, OR run `claude mcp add --scope project ...` / `claude mcp add-json`. Project scope writes here; user/local scopes write to ~/.claude.json instead.
tools.notes: Exact per-server schema (verified): stdio = {"type":"stdio","command":"...","args":[...],"env":{...}}; http = {"type":"http","url":"https://...","headers":{...}}. Supports ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} env expansion. Use ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.} for project-relative paths inside args/command. SSE is legacy/deprecated -> use http. stdio servers MUST NOT console.log (corrupts JSON-RPC on stdout). Scope precedence for MCP: local > project > user; objects are deep-merged across scopes.

tools.name: enabledPlugins (project settings.json key)
tools.whatItDoes: An OBJECT (not array) in settings.json mapping "plugin-id@marketplace-id" -> boolean. Placed in PROJECT .claude/settings.json it activates a globally-cached marketplace plugin ONLY for this project. Confirms the user's core requirement: install cache is global, activation is project-scoped.
tools.installMethod: Add to .claude/settings.json: {"enabledPlugins":{"formatter@acme-tools":true}}. Pair with "extraKnownMarketplaces" so collaborators auto-get the catalog. CLI: `claude plugin install <plugin>@<marketplace> --scope project`.
tools.notes: Schema description verbatim: 'Enabled plugins using plugin-id@marketplace-id format. Example: { "formatter@anthropic-tools": true }'. Value true=enable, false=explicitly disable. KNOWN BUG (anthropics/claude-code#15524): `claude plugin install --scope project` sometimes fails to write the enabledPlugins entry; manual fix is to add the {"plugin@marketplace":true} line yourself. Run /reload-plugins after edits.

tools.name: extraKnownMarketplaces (project settings.json key)
tools.whatItDoes: Object in settings.json declaring plugin marketplaces (e.g. a github repo) so that committing it to project .claude/settings.json makes collaborators auto-install the catalog when they trust the folder. Companion to enabledPlugins for fully self-contained project plugin setup.
tools.installMethod: {"extraKnownMarketplaces":{"acme-tools":{"source":{"source":"github","repo":"acme-corp/claude-plugins"}}}} in .claude/settings.json
tools.notes: Marketplaces + plugins auto-install when the team member trusts the repo folder. This is how you keep plugin activation 100% project-local and reproducible.

tools.name: hooks.PreToolUse (settings.json hook)
tools.whatItDoes: Top-level "hooks" key in settings.json. PreToolUse with matcher "Bash" runs a shell command BEFORE every Bash tool call; the command reads JSON on stdin (.tool_input.command) and can return a deny/ask/allow decision. This is the mechanism to block erase_flash / rm -rf / secret reads.
tools.installMethod: Add to .claude/settings.json hooks block; point command at ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/<script>.sh (keeps it project-local).
tools.notes: Matcher is a CASE-SENSITIVE regex on tool name ('Bash' works, 'bash' does not). hooks hot-reload mid-session (unlike outputStyle). To block, the hook prints to stdout: {"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"PreToolUse","permissionDecision":"deny","permissionDecisionReason":"..."}} and exits 0. permissionDecision accepts allow/deny/ask. Exit code 2 + stderr also blocks (coarser). CAVEAT (anthropics/claude-code#18312): if "Bash" is in permissions.allow, PreToolUse deny/ask may be IGNORED -> do NOT put bare "Bash" in allow if you depend on a deny hook.

tools.name: permissions (allow/ask/deny in settings.json)
tools.whatItDoes: Object with allow/ask/deny arrays of string rules in format Tool or Tool(specifier). deny is evaluated first, then ask, then allow; first match wins. Lets a project pre-deny dangerous Bash patterns and secret reads declaratively without a script.
tools.installMethod: In .claude/settings.json: {"permissions":{"deny":["Read(./.env)","Read(./secrets/**)","Bash(curl *)"],"ask":["Bash(git push *)"],"allow":["Bash(idf.py build)"]}}
tools.notes: IMPORTANT exception to settings precedence: permission rules MERGE across scopes (concatenated+deduped) rather than override. Rule format: Tool(specifier). Use deny for hard blocks (secrets, flash erase), ask for confirm-gated ops. Pairs with the PreToolUse hook for regex-level Bash inspection that static rules can't express.

tools.name: statusLine (settings.json key)
tools.whatItDoes: Object {"type":"command","command":"..."} that runs a script receiving session JSON on stdin and prints the status line. Pointing command at a script inside .claude/ keeps the statusline strictly project-local.
tools.installMethod: {"statusLine":{"type":"command","command":"${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/statusline.sh"}} in .claude/settings.json
tools.notes: Schema: requires type (const 'command') + command; optional padding, refreshInterval (int min 1), hideVimModeIndicator. Project-local by using a repo-relative script path.

tools.name: outputStyle (settings.json key) + .claude/output-styles/
tools.whatItDoes: String key selecting an output style (built-ins: default, Explanatory, Learning). Custom styles dropped in project .claude/output-styles/ are project-local. Adjusts the system prompt.
tools.installMethod: {"outputStyle":"Explanatory"} in .claude/settings.json; custom styles as files under .claude/output-styles/
tools.notes: outputStyle is read ONCE at session start / rebuilt only on /clear or restart (does NOT hot-reload mid-session, unlike hooks/permissions).

tools.name: Project .claude/skills, .claude/agents, .claude/commands (auto-discovery)
tools.whatItDoes: Files placed directly under project .claude/ are auto-discovered with no registration: skills at .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md, subagents at .claude/agents/*.md, slash commands at .claude/commands/*.md. Self-contained and committed with the repo.
tools.installMethod: Create the directories/files under the project's .claude/ folder; discovery is filesystem-based and recursive (subdirs allowed; commands namespace by subdir).
tools.notes: Name-conflict precedence: enterprise > personal(user) > project for skills. If a skill and command share a name, the SKILL takes precedence. Add disable-model-invocation:true in skill frontmatter to make it manual-only. Subdirectory/recursive-discovery detail is partly from third-party blogs; the core auto-discovery of skills/agents/commands under .claude/ is from official docs.

tools.name: settings precedence (4-layer + managed + CLI)
tools.whatItDoes: Defines which settings layer wins. Confirms the user's hypothesized order, with one addition: managed/enterprise sits ABOVE everything and CLI args sit between managed and local.
tools.installMethod: N/A (behavioral). Verify active layers in-session with /status (Setting sources line).
tools.notes: Exact order high->low: (1) Managed/enterprise, (2) CLI args, (3) Local .claude/settings.local.json, (4) Project .claude/settings.json, (5) User ~/.claude/settings.json. Scalars: higher scope wins. Arrays (permissions.allow etc.): MERGE/dedupe. Objects (env, mcpServers): deep-merge. Enterprise lock flags exist: allowManagedPluginsOnly, allowManagedMcpServersOnly, allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly, allowManagedHooksOnly — but these require admin-level managed-settings.json, NOT project-level, so they are out of scope for a project-only harness.

keyAnswers.question: (1) Exact precedence order of the settings layers (highest to lowest)
keyAnswers.answer: Five effective layers, NOT four. Highest -> lowest: (1) Managed/Enterprise (managed-settings.json; on Windows C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\managed-settings.json) — cannot be overridden by anything, even CLI; (2) Command-line arguments (--settings etc.); (3) Local project settings .claude/settings.local.json (gitignored); (4) Shared project settings .claude/settings.json (committed); (5) User settings ~/.claude/settings.json. The user's assumed 'enterprise > user > project > local' order is WRONG on two points: local OUTRANKS project (local is the higher of the two project files), and user is the LOWEST, not above project. Merge semantics: scalars = higher scope wins; arrays (e.g. permissions.allow) = concatenated+deduped across scopes; objects (env, mcpServers, enabledPlugins) = deep-merged. Permission rules specifically merge rather than override.

keyAnswers.question: (2) Can a plugin be enabled per-project via project settings.json enabledPlugins?
keyAnswers.answer: YES. The exact key is "enabledPlugins", an OBJECT (not an array) whose keys are "plugin-id@marketplace-id" strings and values are booleans. Placing it in the PROJECT file .claude/settings.json activates a (globally-cached) marketplace plugin only for that project: install cache is global, activation is project-scoped — exactly the isolation the user needs. Example: {"enabledPlugins":{"formatter@acme-tools":true}}. Pair with "extraKnownMarketplaces" in the same file so collaborators auto-install the catalog on folder trust. Schema description (verbatim from schemastore): 'Enabled plugins using plugin-id@marketplace-id format. Example: { "formatter@anthropic-tools": true }'. Known bug anthropics/claude-code#15524: `claude plugin install --scope project` may not write the entry — add it manually and run /reload-plugins.

keyAnswers.question: (3) Exact PreToolUse hook JSON shape to BLOCK a Bash command matching a regex
keyAnswers.answer: Two parts. CONFIG in .claude/settings.json: {"hooks":{"PreToolUse":[{"matcher":"Bash","hooks":[{"type":"command","command":"${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/block.sh"}]}]}}. The matcher is a case-sensitive regex on the tool name ('Bash', not 'bash'). The SCRIPT reads JSON on stdin, inspects .tool_input.command, and to BLOCK prints this to stdout then exits 0: {"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"PreToolUse","permissionDecision":"deny","permissionDecisionReason":"Destructive command blocked"}}. permissionDecision accepts "allow"|"deny"|"ask". Exit 0 with no output = no decision (normal permission flow continues — silence is NOT approval-bypass). Alternative: exit code 2 with a stderr message also blocks (coarser, less control). CRITICAL CAVEAT (anthropics/claude-code#18312): if "Bash" is listed in permissions.allow, a PreToolUse deny/ask decision is IGNORED — so do not allowlist bare Bash if you rely on this hook to gate flash-erase / rm -rf / secret reads.

keyAnswers.question: How to keep statusline / output-styles / skills strictly project-local
keyAnswers.answer: Reference repo-relative paths so nothing escapes the project. statusLine: {"type":"command","command":"${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/statusline.sh"} in .claude/settings.json (note: ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} is the supported project-root var). outputStyle: set the string in .claude/settings.json and put custom style files in .claude/output-styles/ (read once at session start, does NOT hot-reload). skills/agents/commands: drop files under .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md, .claude/agents/*.md, .claude/commands/*.md — auto-discovered, no registration, committed with the repo. Name-conflict precedence for skills is enterprise > user(personal) > project; a skill beats a command of the same name. hooks and permissions hot-reload mid-session; outputStyle does not.

keyAnswers.question: Project-scoped MCP: is .mcp.json the mechanism, and how does scope precedence work?
keyAnswers.answer: YES — a project-root .mcp.json with a top-level "mcpServers" object is the mechanism (committable, isolated from the user's global ~/.claude.json). Per-server schema: stdio = {"type":"stdio","command":"...","args":[...],"env":{...}} (required: command); http = {"type":"http","url":"https://...","headers":{...}}. Supports ${VAR} / ${VAR:-default} expansion; use ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.} for project-relative paths. SSE transport is deprecated — use http. MCP scope precedence: local > project > user, with objects deep-merged. Write project scope via `claude mcp add --scope project ... -- <command>` (all flags BEFORE the name, then -- before the command) or `claude mcp add-json`. For the embedded use case, the probe-rs/embedded-debugger and context7 servers can be pinned here per-project.
